body:
Why Gujarat became an important trading region

Gujarat occupies an important position on the north-western coast of India. Its coastline faces the Arabian Sea and includes 2 major gulfs: the Gulf of Kachchh and the Gulf of Khambhat. These coastal waters connected settlements in Gujarat with Arabia, the Persian Gulf, the Red Sea region and East Africa.

The importance of Gujarat's ports was not based on their coastal position alone. Rivers, inland roads and trading towns connected the coast with agricultural regions and centres of craft production. The Narmada River, for example, provided a natural connection between the Bharuch region and the interior of western and central India.

A port is a place where vessels can arrive, anchor and exchange goods or passengers. Its hinterland is the inland region connected to the port through roads, rivers and markets. A port that collects goods from different places and redistributes them to other markets is also called an entrepôt.

How the trading system worked

Farmers and craftspeople produced commodities such as cotton cloth, beads, grain and other goods. Merchants collected these products and transported them by carts, pack animals or boats to larger markets. Coastal merchants then arranged their shipment overseas. Imported goods followed the opposite direction: they arrived at a port and could be sold there or carried inland.

Thus, maritime trade and inland trade were closely connected. A successful port required access to useful goods, merchants willing to exchange them and practical arrangements for moving cargo.

Three important historical phases

  • Harappan period: Coastal Gujarat participated in early long-distance exchange. Lothal was an important centre for crafts and maritime connections during the 3rd millennium BCE.
  • Early historic period: Bharuch, known to Greek-speaking traders as Barygaza, became a major port connected with Roman Egypt, West Asia and inland Indian markets. Its importance is especially clear from an account dating to approximately the 1st century CE.
  • Early medieval period: Commercial centres and ports such as Valabhi, Sanjan and, somewhat later, Khambhat and Ghogha became important in changing networks of Indian Ocean trade.

These phases show continuity in Gujarat's participation in overseas commerce, but they should not be treated as a single unchanging trading system. Different ports became prominent in different periods.

Prelims focus

  • Gujarat's 2 major gulfs are the Gulf of Kachchh and the Gulf of Khambhat.
  • The Narmada connected the Bharuch region with inland trade routes.
  • Lothal belongs to the Harappan period; Barygaza is prominent in early historic trade.
  • A hinterland is the inland region economically connected to a port.
  • Trap: A port's overseas exports were not necessarily produced entirely in the port town.

[NCERT, Class 6, Our Pasts–I, 'In the Earliest Cities,' pp. 39–40, and 'Vital Villages, Thriving Towns,' p. 92; NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History, Part I, 'Kings, Farmers and Towns,' pp. 42–44; Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, sections 41–49, W. H. Schoff translation, University of Washington Silk Road text, consulted 19 November 2026.]

title: Gujarat’s Coast and the Foundations of Maritime Trade

body:
One port, several historical names

Bharuch is an ancient trading town in present-day Gujarat, situated on the Narmada River near its approach to the Gulf of Khambhat. It appears in historical literature under several names.

  • Barygaza: The name used in Greek accounts of Indian Ocean commerce.
  • Bharukachchha or Bhrigukachchha: Indian historical forms of the name.
  • Bharuch: The modern name; Broach was another name used in English.

The important distinction is that Barygaza refers to Bharuch, not to the separate town of Khambhat or Cambay. The modern name Gulf of Khambhat does not change the identification of the ancient port.

The account of the Periplus

The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea is an account of maritime routes and markets written by an anonymous Greek-speaking merchant associated with Roman Egypt. It is generally dated to around the middle of the 1st century CE.

The work describes Barygaza as an important commercial destination and gives practical details about reaching it. It refers to the river leading to the port by the name Nammadus, corresponding to the Narmada.

Why ships needed experienced local pilots

The Gulf of Khambhat and the approaches to the Narmada posed serious navigational difficulties. The account describes strong tidal currents, shallow areas, sandbanks and a difficult river entrance. During the change between high and low tide, the movement of water could be especially dangerous for ships unfamiliar with the area.

Experienced local fishermen, serving the ruler, guided incoming vessels through the difficult passages. They could lead or tow ships between shoals and use suitable tidal conditions to move them toward the port. This service reduced the danger of ships running aground.

Barygaza was a river-linked seaport. Its importance came from access to the Arabian Sea and inland Indian markets, while its difficult tidal approach made local navigational knowledge valuable.

The commercial importance of the port

Merchants arriving at Barygaza could obtain cotton textiles, beads, ivory and other commodities brought from different parts of India. They could also sell imported metals, wine and luxury goods. The port therefore acted as a meeting place between overseas shipping and inland commercial routes.

The presence of royal personnel assisting ships also shows that rulers had an interest in the functioning of important trading centres. It does not mean that the ruler personally conducted every transaction or owned every vessel.

Prelims focus

  • Barygaza is the Greek name associated with Bharuch.
  • Bharuch is situated on the Narmada River in Gujarat.
  • The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea is generally dated to the 1st century CE.
  • Local fishermen in the ruler's service helped guide vessels through difficult tidal waters.
  • Trap: Barygaza and Khambhat are not 2 names for the same town.

[NCERT, Class 6, Our Pasts–I, 'Vital Villages, Thriving Towns,' p. 92; Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, sections 41–46, W. H. Schoff translation, University of Washington Silk Road text, consulted 19 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Ships reached Barygaza on the Narmada through tidal currents, shallows and sandbanks, guided along safe passages by local fishermen.
pictures.caption: The hazards and assistance involved in reaching Barygaza.

title: Bharuch or Barygaza: The Great Port of the Narmada

body:
Why an overseas port depended on inland towns

Barygaza was an important outlet for goods produced or collected far from the coast. A maritime merchant could purchase a large variety of products at Bharuch because inland merchants had already carried them there from other regions.

The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea identifies several inland centres associated with the commercial network of Barygaza. Their historical names are particularly useful for matching questions.

Important inland centres and their goods

Ancient nameModern identificationGoods connected with Barygaza
OzeneUjjain, Madhya PradeshAgate, carnelian, muslins and other cloth
Pathana or PaethanaPaithan, MaharashtraCarnelian and other merchandise
TagaraGenerally identified with Ter, MaharashtraCommon cloth, muslins and other textiles

Ujjain was an important inland commercial centre. Goods brought from Ujjain and regions farther inland could reach Barygaza for export. Paithan and Tagara belonged to the Deccan's inland trading network. The ancient account specifically mentions goods being carried from these markets to Barygaza in wagons.

How products moved from production centres to the sea

Textiles might pass from weavers to local merchants, then to a larger inland market, and finally to Barygaza. Semi-precious stones followed a similar commercial route after being collected or worked into valuable objects.

The port's export list therefore included both products associated with western India and goods brought from more distant regions. Barygaza was a place where merchandise was assembled for trade; it was not necessarily the place where every exported commodity originated.

Remember the geographic distinction: Ozene, Pathana and Tagara were inland commercial centres. Barygaza was the maritime outlet through which goods from these centres could enter overseas trade.

Prelims focus

  • Ozene is identified with Ujjain.
  • Pathana or Paethana is identified with Paithan.
  • Tagara is generally identified with Ter.
  • The Periplus describes goods reaching Barygaza from inland centres by wagons.
  • Agate and carnelian were important commodities associated with this trading network.
  • Trap: Ujjain, Paithan and Tagara were not seaports of Gujarat.

[Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, sections 48 and 51, W. H. Schoff translation, University of Washington Silk Road text, consulted 19 November 2026; NCERT, Class 12, Themes in Indian History, Part I, 'Kings, Farmers and Towns,' pp. 43–44.]

pictures.caption: Inland market towns supplied cargo to Barygaza for overseas exchange.

title: The Inland Trade Routes That Supplied Barygaza

body:
Understanding the direction of trade

In trade, an import is a commodity brought into a market from outside, while an export is a commodity sent from that market to another region. For Barygaza, the distinction is important because the same port received foreign goods and shipped Indian goods overseas.

The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea provides a detailed description of the merchandise associated with Barygaza. The following categories preserve the main distinctions in its account.

Major commodities recorded at Barygaza

DirectionCategoryImportant commodities
ImportsMetalsCopper, tin and lead
ImportsLuxury and other goodsWine, coral, topaz, glass, clothing and ornaments
ImportsMoneyGold and silver coins
ExportsTextilesCotton cloth, silk cloth and yarn
ExportsStones and animal productsAgate, carnelian and ivory
ExportsSpices and aromaticsLong pepper, spikenard, costus and bdellium

Why these goods were traded

Cotton cloth and other textiles

Cloth was an important Indian commercial product because it could be transported to distant markets. Different grades of cotton cloth were exchanged, and Barygaza also handled silk textiles and yarn. Some textiles arrived from inland production centres such as Ujjain and Tagara.

Agate and carnelian

Agate and carnelian are varieties of semi-precious stone used for beads and ornaments. Gujarat and neighbouring regions were associated with the working and circulation of such stones. Their value in trade came from their use as ornaments and other crafted objects.

Spices, medicinal plants and aromatics

The exports of Barygaza included long pepper and aromatic substances such as spikenard, costus and bdellium. These products illustrate how a port could distribute valuable goods collected from distant inland regions.

Long pepper should be distinguished from the black pepper strongly associated with the Malabar coast of southern India. Roman demand for pepper was important to Indian Ocean commerce, but that does not mean all pepper came from Gujarat.

Imported metals, wine and coins

Imported copper, tin and lead could be used as raw materials for making objects. Wine, coral and certain kinds of fine clothing were among the goods desired by wealthy purchasers. Gold and silver coins were also brought to Barygaza and could be exchanged for local money.

The ancient account separately mentions special gifts presented to the ruler. Such gifts illustrate the relationship between foreign merchants and political authority, but royal gifts should not be confused with the ordinary merchandise sold in the market.

A port could redistribute goods from many places

One of the most important features of Barygaza was its ability to combine goods from different sources. Indian merchants could bring textiles, beads and aromatics from the interior, while overseas merchants arrived with metals, wine and other products. Some imported goods could then move onward to inland markets.

Prelims focus

  • Wine, copper, tin, lead, coral and gold or silver coins were among the imports of Barygaza.
  • Cotton cloth, silk cloth, agate, carnelian and ivory were among its exports.
  • Long pepper, spikenard, costus and bdellium were also listed among exports.
  • Some exported commodities reached Barygaza from inland markets.
  • Trap: Gold and silver coins appear among the imports in the Periplus account; carnelian appears among its exports.

[NCERT, Class 6, Our Pasts–I, 'Vital Villages, Thriving Towns,' p. 92, and 'Traders, Kings and Pilgrims,' p. 99; Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, sections 48–49 and 56, W. H. Schoff translation, University of Washington Silk Road text, consulted 19 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Barygaza connected inland supply, overseas exports and foreign imports.

title: Imports and Exports of Barygaza
